Should you replace your job management software?

A practical framework for trade businesses weighing up integrations, a different platform or a custom job management app.

By Ben Young · Business owner & AI consultant
Updated 16 November 2026

On this page
  • Write down what isn’t working
  • Compare three routes
  • Count the ongoing costs
  • Check the exit before choosing the destination
  • Move in stages
  • Ask who owns the next improvement

Replacing job management software is a business decision as much as a technical one. The subscription bill is visible; the time spent on workarounds, migration and ongoing support is easier to overlook. Compare the whole picture before deciding.

Write down what isn’t working

Be specific. Is scheduling awkward? Are job notes hard to find? Does the office re-enter data? Are you paying for several overlapping tools? Separate missing features from configuration or training problems. A change to the existing setup may solve more than you expect.

Compare three routes

  • Improve what you have: adjust processes, configuration or team training.
  • Connect or extend it: integrate existing tools or build a small app around a missing workflow.
  • Replace it: move to another platform or build a custom system when the case is strong enough.

Count the ongoing costs

Compare subscriptions with build costs, hosting, AI usage, maintenance, support and future changes. Include the time your team will spend testing and learning. In my own business I removed over $80,000 in annual subscriptions, but that figure is subscription spend removed, not a calculation of net savings after running a custom app.

Check the exit before choosing the destination

Find out what the current platform can export, in what format and with which attachments. Check how customer records, job histories, photos and documents are linked. Do this before cancelling access or committing to a migration date.

Move in stages

  1. Define the records and workflows the new system must support.
  2. Test an export and import using a representative sample.
  3. Check totals, attachments, permissions and relationships between records.
  4. Trial real work with a small group and resolve the problems they find.
  5. Agree a cutover plan, backup and rollback approach.
  6. Keep access to the historical information your business needs.

Ask who owns the next improvement

Before committing, agree how future changes are requested, scoped and supported. For a custom system, clarify source-code access, documentation, data ownership and how another developer could take over.

The right decision may be to keep your current system. I help Melbourne businesses assess the practical options and build a solution when the case makes sense. Read what changed in my own business.
